st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses minimum professional indemnity insurance terms, including coverage, sanctions, policy conditions and reimbursement for misconduct. It does not discuss legal AI’s jagged capabilities, selective deployment, human verification or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: AI insurance: Exclusions operate beyond negligent hallucinations
st.an: The SRA terms support the cluster’s proposition by showing that regulatory policy wording—not lawyer competence or AI error—determines available exclusions, defence-cost protection, aggregation and claimant safeguards. Although the source does not expressly assess AI, its mandatory coverage architecture demonstrates how legal risk can be allocated independently of negligent hallucinations.

kp.k: Mandatory insurance covers private-practice civil liability
kp.d: The MTC require indemnification for civil liability arising from private legal practice connected with the insured firm's practice, including prior practice and, subject to run-off arrangements, successor practice. Cover is triggered by claims first made during the insurance period or claims arising from circumstances first notified during that period. These are insurance requirements, not findings or predictions about AI.

circumstances first notified to the insurer during the period of insurance.

kp.k: Insured status extends beyond current partners and employees
kp.d: Required insureds include the firm, specified owned service and other companies, current and former principals and employees, people joining during the insurance period, and relevant estates or legal representatives. The insurance-specific employee definition includes consultants, agency-type roles and secondees, but excludes contractors required to carry separate professional indemnity insurance for the work.

kp.k: Private practice includes pro bono and ancillary roles
kp.d: The definition extends to services worldwide within the specified authorised practice forms, secondments, employee services and pro bono work. It also includes acting as a personal representative, trustee, attorney, notary or insolvency practitioner in conjunction with a practice, while excluding specified judicial and public appointments.

kp.k: Minimum limits distinguish firms and protect defence funding
kp.d: The minimum sum insured per claim, excluding defence costs, is £3 million for relevant recognised and relevant licensed bodies, with the latter limited to SRA-regulated activities, and £2 million otherwise. Defence costs have no monetary limit, although proportional restriction is permitted where a claim exceeds the sum insured. Other monetary limits, including aggregate limits, are prohibited except as expressly permitted; specified related claims may be treated as one claim.
qs: at least £3 million, and in all other cases, at least £2 million.

kp.k: Excess arrangements preserve claimant and defence protections
kp.d: Insurer and firm may agree an excess, but it must not reduce the required liability limit or apply to defence costs. If an insured fails to pay a claimant an excess amount within 30 days of its becoming due, the claimant can notify the insurer, which must remedy the default. That payment may erode the sum insured, with reinstatement required to the extent it is reimbursed.
qs: The excess must not apply to defence costs.

kp.k: Insurers cannot avoid policies or freely deny liability
kp.d: The policy must prohibit avoidance or repudiation even for fraudulent misrepresentation or breach of the duty of fair presentation. Reduction or denial of liability is confined to permitted exclusions. Cancellation is limited to specified circumstances; claimant payments cannot be offset against premiums or other insured debts; and retroactive-date restrictions are prohibited. Inconsistent policy terms must be severed or rectified to comply with the MTC.

kp.k: Defence funding continues subject to specified safeguards
kp.d: Defence cover includes covered claims, notified circumstances and related investigations or inquiries, but excludes SRA or Tribunal disciplinary proceedings. Costs must be advanced as incurred, including for an insured accused of dishonesty, until the specified admission or judicial finding. During coverage disputes, the SRA may direct claims handling, defence funding and appropriate settlement if reasonable resolution efforts, a reasonable prospect of insured success, and fairness conditions are satisfied.

kp.k: Renewal failure and closure trigger continuing cover
kp.d: Absent qualifying replacement insurance effective immediately after policy expiry, mandatory extended cover lasts up to 30 days, followed by a cessation period ending no later than 90 days after the extended period began, subject to earlier replacement or cessation. Required run-off extends the insurance period for an additional six years, including the extended and cessation periods. Run-off triggered by cessation-period expiry does not cover regulated insureds' subsequent acts or omissions. Transfer to another approved regulator can avoid this run-off requirement where the specified switching protocol applies.

kp.k: Succession rules allocate legacy practice insurance
kp.d: Before cessation, a firm with a successor practice may elect run-off or coverage as a prior practice under the successor's compliant insurance. Failure to elect or pay the required premium before cessation leads to the successor-insurance route. Successor status can arise through holding out, specified movements of principals, and combinations of continuity in name, premises, goodwill, assets, liabilities or staff. Restarted practices may have run-off cancelled only with compliant continuity cover and the required written confirmation.

kp.k: Permitted exclusions retain important legal-work protections
kp.d: Permitted exclusions address prior cover, bodily injury, property damage, internal partnership and employment disputes, trading liabilities, fines and specified penalties, directors' liabilities, war, terrorism and asbestos. Several retain express protection for liabilities arising from legal work, including psychological injury or emotional distress caused by breach of duty. Sanctions provisions bar cover or benefits to the extent they would expose the insurer to specified international or national sanctions.

kp.d: Dishonesty or fraud may exclude indemnity for the person committing or condoning it, but other insureds must remain covered. Corporate attribution requires commission or condonation by all company directors or all LLP members, rather than attribution from an individual alone.
qs: the insurance must nonetheless cover each other insured;
all directors of that company, or in the case of an LLP, all members of that LLP.

kp.k: Claimant protection coexists with insurer reimbursement rights
kp.d: Policies may allow just and equitable reimbursement for specified knowing or reckless misrepresentation, breaches and dishonesty, and for cessation-period activity outside the permitted existing-instructions work. Regulatory-compliance breaches are protected from reimbursement to the stated extent. Separate provisions permit recovery of defence costs or dispute-related payments ultimately not owed, and excess payments from specified principals. Thus restrictions on denying cover do not eliminate insureds' potential repayment obligations.

kp.k: Compensation coverage differs from fee refunds and sanctions
kp.d: Amounts payable pursuant to recommendations of the Office for Legal Complaints or other regulatory authorities must be covered to the same extent as civil liability, but specified Legal Ombudsman fee-refund determinations are excluded. The definition of claim also treats obligations to remedy SRA Accounts Rules breaches as claims without requiring a compensation demand, subject to the stated bank or building-society failure exceptions.

kp.k: Premiums may reflect practice characteristics and risk
kp.d: The insurer and firm may agree premium calculation based on claims history, work categories, numbers of principals and employees, practice revenue and other insurer-determined risk factors. The MTC and connected disputes are governed by the law and courts of England and Wales.
